## Study objective and approach

- Examine how tuning parameters affect prediction accuracy.
- Change one parameter at a time, comparing each setting with the same baseline.
- Reset to the baseline for each experiment; improvements are not carried forward.

## Data and preprocessing

- One row represents a product's selling episode on the website.
- Predict **quantity** from SKU, price, order, duration, and category.
- Random row split: **70% training / 15% validation / 15% test**, seed 42.
- Fit min-max scaling and category/SKU mappings on training data only.
- Scale numeric inputs and quantity, one-hot encode category, and embed SKU in eight dimensions.
- Load the CSV in chunks of **16,384 rows** for incremental training.

Repeated SKUs can occur across splits. The comparison concerns held-out episodes, including episodes for products seen in training.

## Training and evaluation

- Every logged run trains for **20 epochs**, using random seed **42**.
- Shuffle training observations within each chunk and update by mini-batch.
- Evaluate validation MSE after each epoch and restore the best weights.
- Keep the learning rate constant within a run. No early stopping.
- Report validation metrics on **75,053 observations**. RMSE and MAE use the supplied quantity scale.

**Source:** We tested a total of 31 configurations ran on both October 30 and 31. Scores match across dates. Tables use October 31 throughout, including runtime.

These repeated runs use the same seed and do not measure variability across seeds. The CSV contains validation results only.

## Baseline model

Three sigmoid hidden layers: **21 / 12 / 7 neurons**. Eight-dimensional SKU embedding, one-hot category, scaled numeric inputs, and a linear output.

| Setting | Value |
|:---|:---|
| Optimizer / learning rate | Adam / 0.001 |
| Batch size | 1,024 |
| Selected epoch | 19 |

| Validation $R^2$ | MSE | RMSE | MAE |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.3852 | 1,612.48 | 40.16 | 21.40 |

All following $\Delta R^2$ values compare with this baseline. Positive values indicate improvement.

## Batch size

| Batch size | Validation $R^2$ | RMSE | $\Delta R^2$ | Seconds |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32 | 0.5210 | 35.44 | +0.1358 | 187.4 |
| 128 | 0.5277 | 35.20 | +0.1425 | 61.2 |
| 256 | 0.4304 | 38.65 | +0.0452 | 39.6 |
| 512 | 0.4102 | 39.33 | +0.0250 | 28.5 |
| 1024 (baseline) | 0.3852 | 40.16 | +0.0000 | 22.9 |

**Finding:** Batch 128 has the highest validation $R^2$ in this comparison, but takes about 2.7 times the baseline runtime.

**Interpretation:** Smaller batches make more weight updates per epoch. This comparison includes that extra optimization work. Runtime covers preprocessing and the training loop, including validation.

## Number of hidden layers

| Hidden layers and neurons | Validation $R^2$ | RMSE | $\Delta R^2$ |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1: 21 | 0.3667 | 40.76 | -0.0185 |
| 2: 21 / 12 | 0.3591 | 41.00 | -0.0261 |
| 3: 21 / 12 / 7 (baseline) | 0.3852 | 40.16 | +0.0000 |
| 4: 21 / 12 / 7 / 4 | 0.4023 | 39.59 | +0.0171 |
| 5: 21 / 12 / 7 / 4 / 2 | 0.2513 | 44.31 | -0.1339 |

**Finding:** Four layers improve $R^2$ slightly. Five layers perform substantially worse.

**Interpretation:** Extra depth does not guarantee better predictions. The narrow added layers also change capacity, so this result applies to these specific architectures.

## Neurons per hidden layer

| Three-layer architecture | Validation $R^2$ | RMSE | $\Delta R^2$ |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| 21 / 12 / 7 (baseline) | 0.3852 | 40.16 | +0.0000 |
| 8 / 8 / 8 | 0.3884 | 40.05 | +0.0032 |
| 16 / 16 / 16 | 0.3909 | 39.97 | +0.0057 |
| 32 / 32 / 32 | 0.3549 | 41.13 | -0.0302 |
| 64 / 64 / 64 | 0.4145 | 39.19 | +0.0293 |
| 128 / 128 / 128 | 0.2915 | 43.11 | -0.0937 |

**Finding:** The 64 / 64 / 64 network performs best among the tested widths. The widest network performs worse than the baseline.

**Interpretation:** More neurons change capacity and optimization. Scores do not improve steadily with width. These trials also replace the baseline's taper with equal-width layers.

## Hidden activation function

| Activation | Validation $R^2$ | RMSE | $\Delta R^2$ |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| Sigmoid (baseline) | 0.3852 | 40.16 | +0.0000 |
| ReLU | 0.4526 | 37.89 | +0.0675 |
| Tanh | 0.3582 | 41.03 | -0.0270 |
| ELU | 0.4057 | 39.48 | +0.0205 |

**Finding:** ReLU gives the largest gain in this comparison. Tanh reduces $R^2$.

**Interpretation:** ReLU avoids sigmoid's positive-side saturation, which can help gradient flow. This is a possible explanation for the gain, not a measured gradient result.

The output layer remains linear for quantity regression.

## Optimizer

| Optimizer | Validation $R^2$ | RMSE | $\Delta R^2$ |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| Adam (baseline) | 0.3852 | 40.16 | +0.0000 |
| SGD | -0.1866 | 55.79 | -0.5718 |
| AdaGrad | -0.1838 | 55.72 | -0.5690 |
| RMSprop | 0.1002 | 48.58 | -0.2850 |

**Finding:** Adam performs best with the shared learning rate of **0.001**. SGD and AdaGrad have negative validation $R^2$.

Negative $R^2$ means greater squared error than predicting the validation-set mean.

**Interpretation:** Optimizers behave differently at the same learning rate. These runs compare a shared setting rather than each optimizer's best possible tuning.

## Learning rate

| Adam learning rate | Validation $R^2$ | RMSE | $\Delta R^2$ |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.00001 | -0.1105 | 53.97 | -0.4957 |
| 0.0001 | 0.2903 | 43.14 | -0.0949 |
| 0.0005 | 0.3969 | 39.77 | +0.0118 |
| 0.001 (baseline) | 0.3852 | 40.16 | +0.0000 |
| 0.005 | 0.3626 | 40.89 | -0.0226 |
| 0.01 | 0.4860 | 36.71 | +0.1009 |
| 0.1 | 0.4783 | 36.99 | +0.0931 |

**Finding:** 0.01 performs best among these rates. The smallest rate produces negative $R^2$.

**Interpretation:** A very small rate may learn too slowly within the shared training budget. Larger rates help here, but the relationship is not monotonic.

## Sensitivity findings

| Comparison | Highest observed setting | Validation $R^2$ |
|:---|:---|---:|
| Batch size | 128 | 0.5277 |
| Hidden layers | 4: 21 / 12 / 7 / 4 | 0.4023 |
| Hidden neurons | 64 / 64 / 64 | 0.4145 |
| Activation | ReLU | 0.4526 |
| Optimizer | Adam (baseline) | 0.3852 |
| Learning rate | 0.01 | 0.4860 |

Learning rate and optimizer produce the largest observed spreads in $R^2$ across their tested settings.

Each row summarizes a separate comparison against baseline $R^2$ **0.3852**. These settings were not combined or confirmed as a final model.

## Scope and limitations

- One seed and one split limit conclusions about repeatability.
- Equal epochs give smaller batches more updates. Runtime also varies.
- Validation selects the best epoch and supports these comparisons. A final test score is absent from the CSV.
- Independent comparisons do not measure interactions, such as ReLU with a different learning rate.
- Learning-rate schedules, dropout, L2, gradient clipping, and sequence models are outside these logged comparisons.

**Conclusion:** Performance is sensitive to tuning choices. More layers, more neurons, or a smaller learning rate do not consistently improve validation results.
